newsitem.title: USA: Ad group works to end kid tobacco marketing.
newsitem.headline: Ad group works to end kid tobacco marketing.

text.p: The Clinton administration's proposals to restrict tobacco advertising were opposed by many on Madison Avenue, but a small group of ad executives Wednesday will launch a campaign to end cigarette marketing to children.

The Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids is calling on the ad industry to set its own curbs on marketing cigarettes to young people, in an effort that will be announced officially at a news briefing Wednesday.

The group concedes that it is unlikely to get much support from the biggest ad agencies, especially since key trade organisations have already joined the opposition. But it hopes to get rank-and-file support in the industry and spark a debate about the marketing methods being used.
"We're just starting, and we expect we're going to have a lot of participation," said William Novelli, retired chief of the Porter Novelli public relations firm.

"I don't know if the heads of the really big agencies are going to join in. Many of them have billings in U.S. tobacco companies or with subsidiaries of tobacco companies. We may, or may not, get them," he said.

Novelli said the group plans to push for support from within the industry on key issues in the Clinton proposal, including bans on billboard marketings near schools, cigarette advertising in teen magazines and special promotions to put cigarette brands on products used by teens.
"If the ad industry can quickly and effectively act to get their house in order, it will help their own image as an industry and it will protect children," said Novelli.

Among those listing their support for the campaign are David Milenthal, chairman of HMS Partners, a $200 million advertising agency, and from two smaller agencies, David McCall, chairman of Shepardson Stern & Kamisnsky and Dan Cronin, account executive at Biderman, Kelly & Shaffer.
But the group listed no supporters from any of the top 50 advertising agencies in the United States.

Novelli said the group will try to persuade more agency executives to support their cause by launching an ad campaign in trade publications and by sponsoring an industry summit to debate the issue. The group will actively seek views from the industry through surveys and study. It also plans to lobby industry organisations directly through letter writing to get support.
